title: How fast? The rate of chemical change
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank, except where marked for IB Diploma Chemistry (status of the source: ai-reviewed-reverified-gate-verified-2026-09-30-awaiting-human-signoff). Terms and clues: R2.2#c01 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition; R2.2#c10 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition; R2.2#c06 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition; R2.2#c03 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition. Questions: R2.2#q01, R2.2#q04, R2.2#q07, R2.2#q09, R2.2#q12, R2.2#q02, R2.2#q05, R2.2#q03, R2.2#q13, R2.2#q15, R2.2#q17, R2.2#q18, R2.2#q20, R2.2#q23.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Rate of reaction
items.clue: The change in concentration of a species per unit time.

items.label: Activation energy, Ea
items.clue: The minimum that colliding particles need for a successful change.

items.label: Collision frequency
items.clue: The number of encounters between particles per unit time in a given volume.

items.label: Collision theory
items.clue: The model in which particles must meet with enough energy and the correct orientation.

questions.stem: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes: 2H₂O₂(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g). Which quantity is the rate of this reaction at a particular moment?

options.text: The total time taken for all of the H₂O₂ in the sample to decompose
The total volume of O₂ given off by the time the reaction has stopped
The decrease in the concentration of H₂O₂ per unit time at that moment
The concentration of H₂O₂ at that moment divided by the time elapsed so far

questions.explanation: Rate is the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time, in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. At a particular moment it is the gradient of the tangent to the concentration–time curve, quoted as a positive value for the decrease in [H₂O₂].

questions.stem: Sample P is neon gas at 40 °C. Sample Q contains twice as many krypton atoms as P and is at 20 °C. Which statement comparing the kinetic energies of the atoms in the two samples is correct?

options.text: The mean kinetic energy of the atoms in P is greater than that in Q, but only by about 7%.
The mean kinetic energy of the atoms in P is twice the mean kinetic energy in Q.
The atoms in Q have the greater mean kinetic energy, as krypton atoms are heavier.
The atoms in Q have the greater mean kinetic energy, as Q contains more atoms.

questions.explanation: Mean kinetic energy is proportional to the absolute temperature: 40 °C = 313 K and 20 °C = 293 K, so the ratio is 313/293 = 1.07. The size of the sample does not affect the mean energy per atom. Neither the number of atoms nor their mass affects the mean kinetic energy per atom.

questions.stem: Hydrogen iodide decomposes: 2HI(g) → H₂(g) + I₂(g). A sample of hydrogen iodide is compressed to half its volume at constant temperature. What is the effect on the rate of reaction, and why?

options.text: It is unchanged: there are equal amounts of gas on both sides of the equation, so pressure has no effect.
It increases: the compressed molecules collide more energetically, so more collisions exceed Ea.
It increases: a larger amount of H₂ and I₂ can now form from the same amount of HI as before.
It increases: collisions become more frequent, and the fraction with E ≥ Ea is unchanged.

questions.stem: For a reaction with Ea = 50 kJ mol⁻¹, raising the temperature from 300 K to 310 K almost doubles the rate. Which statement gives the main reason for this large increase?

options.text: A much larger fraction of all the collisions now have energy equal to or greater than Ea.
The particles move faster, so they collide more often, and more collisions give more reactions.
The activation energy decreases as the temperature rises, so more of the collisions succeed.
Every particle gains the same amount of energy, which carries many more of them past Ea.

questions.stem: For a hypothetical endothermic reaction, the uncatalysed forward activation energy is 280 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔH = +110 kJ mol⁻¹. A catalyst lowers the forward activation energy to 230 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the activation energy of the catalysed reverse reaction?

options.text: +170 kJ mol⁻¹
−110 kJ mol⁻¹
+120 kJ mol⁻¹
+340 kJ mol⁻¹

questions.explanation: The products lie 110 kJ mol⁻¹ above the reactants and the catalysed maximum lies 230 kJ mol⁻¹ above the reactants, so the reverse barrier is 230 − 110 = 120 kJ mol⁻¹. The catalyst lowers the forward and reverse activation energies by the same 50 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.stem: Magnesium ribbon reacts with excess hydrochloric acid, and the hydrogen is collected in a gas syringe. A graph of the volume of hydrogen (y-axis, cm³) against time (x-axis, s) is a curve that is steep at first, becomes less steep and levels off at 60 cm³ at 100 s. The curve passes through the point (20 s, 34 cm³). A tangent drawn to the curve at t = 20 s passes through the points (0 s, 10 cm³) and (40 s, 58 cm³). What is the rate of reaction at t = 20 s?

options.text: 1.70 cm³ s⁻¹
0.60 cm³ s⁻¹
0.83 cm³ s⁻¹
1.20 cm³ s⁻¹

questions.stem: Two reactant molecules in a gas collide with a combined kinetic energy greater than the activation energy, Ea, of the reaction, but they do not react. Which statement explains this?

options.text: No catalyst was present, and a reaction cannot take place at all without one.
They collided with an orientation that did not bring the reacting atoms together.
Their combined energy was less than the size of the enthalpy change of reaction, ΔH.
No spark or heating had first supplied the activation energy to start the reaction.

questions.explanation: A successful collision needs both energy equal to or greater than Ea and a proper orientation. With enough energy but the wrong collision geometry, the atoms that must bond do not meet, so no reaction occurs.

questions.stem: The concentration of a reactant, R, is followed at constant temperature. A graph of [R] (y-axis, mol dm⁻³) against time (x-axis, s) is a curve that starts at 0.0500 mol dm⁻³, becomes less steep and reaches zero at 1500 s. The curve passes through the point (300 s, 0.0220 mol dm⁻³). A tangent drawn to the curve at t = 300 s passes through the points (0 s, 0.0370 mol dm⁻³) and (600 s, 0.0070 mol dm⁻³). What is the rate of reaction at t = 300 s?

options.text: 7.33 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
5.00 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
3.33 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
9.33 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

questions.stem: Nitrogen monoxide reacts with hydrogen: 2NO(g) + 2H₂(g) → N₂(g) + 2H₂O(g). The experimentally determined rate equation is rate = k[NO]²[H₂]. Which proposed mechanism is consistent with both the rate equation and the overall equation?

options.text: 2NO → N₂O₂ (slow); N₂O₂ + H₂ → N₂ + H₂O₂; H₂O₂ + H₂ → 2H₂O (both fast)
2NO ⇌ N₂O₂ (fast); N₂O₂ + H₂ → N₂ + H₂O₂ (slow); H₂O₂ → 2OH (fast)
2NO + 2H₂ → N₂ + 2H₂O as a single step, in one collision of all four molecules
2NO ⇌ N₂O₂ (fast); N₂O₂ + H₂ → N₂O + H₂O (slow); N₂O + H₂ → N₂ + H₂O (fast)

questions.explanation: The steps add up to 2NO + 2H₂ → N₂ + 2H₂O once the intermediates N₂O₂ and N₂O cancel. The slow second step involves N₂O₂ (formed from 2NO in the fast first step) and H₂, so the rate equation is rate = k[NO]²[H₂]. Here the rate-determining step is not the first step.

questions.stem: A reaction occurs in two steps. Its energy profile, with energies relative to the reactants, shows: reactants 0 kJ mol⁻¹; a first maximum at +45 kJ mol⁻¹; a minimum at +15 kJ mol⁻¹; a second maximum at +80 kJ mol⁻¹; products −20 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the activation energy of the rate-determining step?

options.text: +65 kJ mol⁻¹
+45 kJ mol⁻¹
+80 kJ mol⁻¹
−35 kJ mol⁻¹

questions.stem: Which statement about molecularity is correct?

options.text: 2NO(g) → N₂O₂(g) is a unimolecular step.
N₂O₄(g) → 2NO₂(g) is a termolecular step.
2NO₂(g) → NO₃(g) + NO(g) is a bimolecular step.
Overall, 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(g) is termolecular.

questions.explanation: Two NO₂ molecules collide in this elementary step, so two reacting particles take part and it is bimolecular. The products are not counted.

questions.stem: A reaction has the overall equation 2A + B → C + D. A student states that its rate equation must be rate = k[A]²[B]. Which response is correct?

options.text: The student is correct, as orders are the coefficients of the reactants in the balanced equation.
The rate equation can only be found by experiment, and its orders need not match the coefficients.
The rate equation must include the products, written as rate = k[C][D]/[A]²[B], like K.
The orders are the coefficients of the reactants in the first step of the mechanism.

questions.stem: A reaction is zero order with respect to reactant X. Which statement about a graph for this reaction is correct?

options.text: The concentration–time graph for X is a straight line with a negative gradient.
The concentration–time graph for X is a horizontal line, as X is not used up in the reaction.
The rate–concentration graph for X is a straight line sloping downwards, with a negative gradient.
The rate–concentration graph for X is a straight line through the origin, as rate rises with [X].

questions.explanation: For a zero-order reactant the rate does not depend on [X], so X is used up at a constant rate and its concentration falls in a straight line until it is used up.

questions.stem: The rate equation for a reaction is rate = k[A]², with concentrations in mol dm⁻³ and the rate in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. What are the units of k?

options.text: mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹, as the rate constant has the same units as the rate
mol⁻¹ dm³ s⁻¹, as k = rate/[A]² for a second-order reaction
s⁻¹, as only one reactant, A, appears in the rate equation
mol³ dm⁻⁹ s⁻¹, as k = rate × [A]² when the rate equation is rearranged

questions.explanation: k = rate/[A]², so its units are (mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹)/(mol dm⁻³)² = mol⁻¹ dm³ s⁻¹, the units for any reaction that is second order overall.
